questions.q: Why doesn't AWS CloudShell require you to run `aws configure` before using it?
options: You still must run aws configure, it just hides the prompts
CloudShell doesn't actually run real AWS CLI commands
It's pre-authenticated — it inherits the IAM permissions of whichever console user launched it
CloudShell only works with the root account, which never needs credentials
questions.explain: CloudShell is launched from inside the console you're already signed into, so it inherits that session's permissions.

questions.q: Besides being pre-authenticated, what else is already set up when AWS CloudShell opens?
options: A permanent EC2 instance is created just for that session
Nothing — every tool must be installed manually each time
The AWS CLI, Python, and several other common tools are already installed
Only a text editor, with no command-line tools at all
questions.explain: CloudShell runs in a small container with the CLI and common tools pre-installed, so there's nothing to set up first.

questions.q: How much persistent storage does CloudShell give each user, and where?
options: 10 GB, but only for the duration of a single session
Unlimited storage shared across all regions
No persistent storage at all — everything is lost when the session ends
1 GB per AWS Region, under $HOME, surviving between sessions
questions.explain: CloudShell persists 1 GB per Region under $HOME, so saved scripts are still there next time you open it in that region.

questions.q: In the script `for bucket in $(aws s3 ls | awk '{print $3}'); do ... done`, what does `awk '{print $3}'` do?
options: Converts the output into JSON format
Counts the total number of buckets
Pulls just the bucket name (the third column) out of aws s3 ls's output
Deletes the third bucket in the list
questions.explain: aws s3 ls prints bucket name in the third column; awk extracts just that column for the loop to use.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is CloudShell the wrong tool for the job?
options: For any task involving S3
CloudShell has no real limitations and is always the right choice
For scheduled or unattended automation, which belongs in a Lambda function or CI/CD pipeline instead
For any task that uses the AWS CLI at all
questions.explain: CloudShell sessions time out and storage is capped, so scheduled or long-running automation belongs elsewhere.
